reference.kind: norm: researched Milky Way totals; no generator run sets a range
reference.galaxy: a Milky Way-like galaxy drawn through the generator's shape chain (tests.audit.prevalence_phenomena.milky_way_like_shape: 5.2e10 solar masses of stars, disk scale length 2600 pc, thin disk height 300 pc, a fifth of the stars in the bulge, two arms) with the default sector edge; the scatter's own expectation summed over every shell of the outline, with no mass cut

sources.Green2019: Green, A revised catalogue of 294 Galactic supernova remnants (arXiv:1907.02638, read 2026-10-29): 294 catalogued
sources.McGill: Olausen and Kaspi 2014, The McGill Magnetar Catalog (arXiv:1309.4167, read 2026-10-29): 26 known magnetars and candidates
sources.FrewParker: Frew and Parker 2010, Planetary Nebulae: Observational Properties, Mimics, and Diagnostics (arXiv:1002.1525, read 2026-10-29): nearly 3000 true, likely and possible planetary nebulae known
sources.Rosslowe: Rosslowe and Crowther 2015 (arXiv:1412.0699, read 2026-10-29): 1200, +300 and -100, Wolf-Rayet stars in the Galaxy (used by the second cut of the census)
sources.Mroz2017: Mróz et al. 2017, Nature 548:183: at most 0.25 Jupiter-mass free-floating planets per main-sequence star (an upper limit; quoted by tuning.py and docs/design/systems/interstellar-object-rates.md)
sources.Johnson2020: Johnson et al. 2020 (AJ 160:123) and Mróz et al. 2020 (ApJL 903:L11): 2 to 10 terrestrial free-floating planets per star, 0.5 to 1.4 per pc^3 (as docs/design/systems/interstellar-object-rates.md quotes them, recalled and unverified)
sources.Kirkpatrick2021: Kirkpatrick et al. 2021, ApJS 253:7: 0.025 to 0.035 brown dwarfs per pc^3 (as the interstellar-object-rates note quotes it, recalled)
sources.Tauris2015: Tauris 2015, MNRAS 448:L6: stars moving faster than 30 km/s are 1 to 2 percent of stars
sources.DoEngelhardt: Do et al. 2018 and Engelhardt et al. 2017 as the interstellar-object-rates note quotes them: 0.1 to 0.2 interstellar objects of about 100 m and up per au^3, 7e14 to 1.8e15 per pc^3
sources.CantatGaudin2020: Cantat-Gaudin et al. 2020 (arXiv:2004.07274, read 2026-10-29): reliable parameters for 1867 clusters from Gaia DR2, complete only to about 2 kpc
sources.HuntReffert2023: Hunt and Reffert 2023 (arXiv:2303.13424, read 2026-10-29): 7167 clusters in Gaia DR3, as many as a few thousand of them unbound moving groups

anomalies.GEN.995: 890 against 1100 to 1500 (the draws' tolerance puts the edge at 904), counted over the primaries and their companions. The massive stars follow the mass function exactly now (GEN.927 to GEN.930; the 958 before counted every massive star twice, as a primary and again as a companion); what is missing is the Wolf-Rayet stars that binary stripping makes out of stars too light to be one alone, which the generator does not draw

stellar_black_holes.source: about 1e8 (Olejak et al. 2020, A&A 638:A94; Sahu et al. 2022, ApJ 933:83; the figures tuning.py quotes), recalled and unverified (tier T3); the range is a decade either side

neutron_stars.source: about 1e9 (Sartore et al. 2010, A&A 510:A23; the figure tuning.py quotes), recalled and unverified (tier T3); the lower edge is the 1e8 of the lower population estimates

magnetars.source: 26 known (McGill catalog, a floor); 100 active with 30 to 600 estimated (Olausen and Kaspi 2014 as tuning.py quotes it, recalled and unverified)

intermediate_black_holes.source: Boss's decision card of 2026-10-16 (GEN.259): hundreds, as the few candidates suggest; no confirmed one in the field

planetary_nebulae.source: nearly 3000 known (Frew and Parker 2010, a floor); about 20000 galaxy-wide as tuning.py quotes it (recalled and unverified, tier T3); the upper edge twice that

wolf_rayet_stars.source: Rosslowe and Crowther 2015 (arXiv:1412.0699): 1200, +300 and -100, Wolf-Rayet stars in the Galaxy (read 2026-10-29); 322 found since the VIIth catalogue

supernova_remnants.source: 294 catalogued (Green 2019, a floor); 400 to 3000 still visible from the supernova rate (GEN.203, tuning.py), recalled

rogue_terrestrial_per_star.source: 2 to 10 per star (Johnson et al. 2020; Mróz et al. 2020), as docs/design/systems/interstellar-object-rates.md quotes them, recalled and unverified; the generator's rate is the terrestrial bin of tuning.ROGUE_PLANET_MASS_BINS

rogue_terrestrial_per_pc3.source: 0.5 to 1.4 per pc^3 at the solar neighbourhood's stellar density (the same note)

rogue_jupiter_per_star.source: at most 0.25 per star (Mróz et al. 2017, an upper limit); the floor is a stand-in, that some are found (Mróz 2017 detected a population)

brown_dwarfs_per_pc3.source: 0.025 to 0.035 per pc^3 (Kirkpatrick et al. 2021), as the interstellar-object-rates note quotes it

runaway_stars_per_star.source: 1 to 2 percent of stars faster than 30 km/s (Tauris 2015)

interstellar_debris_per_pc3.source: 7e14 to 1.8e15 per pc^3, 0.1 to 0.2 per au^3 for objects of about 100 m and up (Do et al. 2018; Engelhardt et al. 2017), as the interstellar-object-rates note quotes them, recalled

open_clusters.source: 1867 clusters with reliable parameters from Gaia DR2, a floor complete only to about 2 kpc (Cantat-Gaudin et al. 2020); 7167 candidate clusters in DR3, some thousand of them moving groups (Hunt and Reffert 2023); tens of thousands in all, recalled and unverified (docs/design/galaxy/intergalactic-and-halo-contents.md 5.14); the upper edge is the generator's own cap, tuning.OPEN_CLUSTER_MAX_COUNT
